title: Right to Vote in 'Great Peril,' Justice Nariman Warns as Executive Grip Tightens
excerpt: In a September 27 oration, the former Supreme Court judge cited 90 lakh exclusions in West Bengal's voter-roll revision and called the executive's grip on Election Commissioner appointments a "red flag."
body:
• Former Supreme Court judge Justice Rohinton Fali Nariman has warned that "the heart of our democracy, which is the right to vote, is in great peril" — citing mass voter exclusion and executive control over the Election Commission.
  • In a September 27 speech at Rajkumar College, Rajkot, he said 90 lakh voters were disenfranchised in West Bengal during the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls — and of 1 lakh appeals decided, 93% went in favour of the excluded voters.
  • Nariman called leaving the appointment of Election Commissioners entirely to the government of the day a "red flag", and said the Supreme Court must decide the validity of the CEC Act at the earliest.
  • He also flagged reports that crucial decisions were taken by the Chief Election Commissioner while ignoring the objections of the other two Election Commissioners.

Former Supreme Court judge Justice Rohinton Fali Nariman has delivered one of the sharpest critiques yet of India's electoral machinery, warning that the right to vote — "the heart of the Constitution and the heart of democracy" — is in great peril amid large-scale voter exclusion and creeping executive control over the Election Commission of India.

The speech

Nariman was delivering the Centenary Oration on "The Constitution and the Common Man" at Rajkumar College, Rajkot, on September 27. His central charge: the massive disenfranchisement of voters during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. He noted that 90 lakh voters had been excluded in West Bengal, that 22 lakh affected citizens filed appeals, and that among the 1 lakh appeals decided so far, an overwhelming 93% of verdicts came in favour of the excluded.

"So can you imagine, this was a completely illegal knocking out of the common man, of the citizen of India, in order that a government obtains what it wants."

— Justice Rohinton Fali Nariman, former Supreme Court judge

He added that the West Bengal result "was something that upset the government of the day and brought in the government of the centre," and lamented that the scale of the exclusion had not moved the Supreme Court sufficiently to stay the revision exercise. "You can't have an election commission which functions or malfunctions like this," he said.

The appointments fight

Nariman's second front was structural: who picks the referees. He described leaving the appointment of Election Commissioners entirely in the hands of the government of the day as a "red flag." The reference is to the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, which replaced the Supreme Court's recommended neutral selection panel — the prime minister, the leader of the opposition and the Chief Justice of India, per the Anoop Baranwal judgment — with a panel that substitutes a Union Cabinet minister for the Chief Justice, effectively restoring executive dominance over appointments.

He expressed disappointment that a two-judge Supreme Court bench had delivered a split verdict on the challenge to the appointment process, allowing the government to continue making appointments under the executive-heavy process. The Supreme Court, he said, must decide the validity of the CEC Act at the earliest.

Context

Nariman's remarks land amid a broader storm around the poll body. Reports have suggested that several crucial decisions were taken by the Chief Election Commissioner while ignoring the objections of the other two Election Commissioners. In Mumbai, actors Shabana Azmi and Naseeruddin Shah recently joined a public protest demanding the Election Chief's ouster — a sign that the disquiet Nariman voiced from a Rajkot dais is spilling into the streets.

Diaspora angle

For the diaspora, the stakes are reputational as well as democratic: India's standing as the world's largest democracy rests on the credibility of its elections, and NRIs — who defend that record in parliaments, campuses and boardrooms abroad — have the most to lose when a former Supreme Court judge says the right to vote is in peril. The CEC Act challenge now pending before the court is the case to watch.
